A plugin extends a board as a whole, as the DAG of blockr.dag does, and its class comes from a package (see `?blockr.core::new_plugin`).
Where the class has a `ui`, every frontend places that UI on the page, and the dock places it in a panel.
This vignette is for the author of such a package.
It says how a plugin draws in its panel and sizes itself there, where it opens what needs more room, how it shows a block or a plugin, how it reads the dock's state and changes which views hold which panels, and where its settings go.
Its last section names what else the dock draws for plugins.

The examples follow one plugin class, which a package blockr.notes ships under the id `blockr.notes-notes_plugin`.
Its plugin keeps notes about the board's blocks, and lists them in its panel.
The package is made up for this vignette.

## A plugin class with a UI

A package defines a plugin class in a JS module of its own.
The module exports the major of core's JS API that it was built against, and the class without its id as its default.
Core registers the class under the id that R gives it, `{pkg}-{id}`.
Core's types describe each member of a class, as the interface `PluginClass`.
The function `install_js_types()` of blockr.core installs them under the name `@blockr/core`, as the vignette on block classes describes (`vignette("create-block", package = "blockr.core")`).

The Notes plugin keeps its notes in its state, and its `ui` lists them:

```ts
import type { JsonSchema, PluginClass } from "@blockr/core";
import schema from "./notes.schema.json" with { type: "json" };

type Note = { readonly block: string; readonly text: string };
type State = { readonly notes: readonly Note[] };

export const api = 1;

export default {
  state: { schema: schema as JsonSchema, default: { notes: [] } },
  ui: {
    render({ el, core, plugin }) {
      const list = document.createElement("ul");
      list.className = "notes";
      el.replaceChildren(list);
      const draw = (): void => {
        const { notes } = core.store.board().plugins[plugin] as State;
        list.replaceChildren(
          ...notes.map((note) => {
            const block = document.createElement("span");
            block.className = "note-block";
            block.textContent = note.block;
            const item = document.createElement("li");
            item.append(note.text, " ", block);
            return item;
          }),
        );
      };
      draw();
      return core.store.subscribe(draw);
    },
  },
} satisfies Omit<PluginClass, "id">;
```

Core calls `render()` with the element to draw in, `CoreApi`, the id of the plugin's class and a signal.
The function may return its cleanup, here the end of the subscription to the board.

In R, the package gives a constructor of its plugins and lists the class in the `._BLOCKR_MODULES_` that it exports, with the class's name and its module (see `?blockr.core::read_blocks_yml`):

```r
#' @export
new_notes_plugin <- function(notes = list()) {
  blockr.core::new_plugin(list(notes = notes), "notes_plugin")
}

#' @export
._BLOCKR_MODULES_ <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())

.onLoad <- function(libname, pkgname) {
  ._BLOCKR_MODULES_$plugins <- list(
    new_notes_plugin = list(
      id = "notes_plugin",
      name = "Notes",
      module = "js/notes.js"
    )
  )
}
```

The schema of the state ships beside the module, as `js/notes.schema.json`, and R writes the state that an app script gives the plugin by it.
An app runs every plugin class that `blockr.core::available_plugins()` gives, unless its script names the plugins in the `plugins` of `serve()`.
So the Notes plugin runs in every app where blockr.notes is installed.

## The panel

The dock offers each plugin whose class has a `ui` one panel, in which it mounts the plugin's UI with `core.mountPlugin()`.
A view shows each plugin's panel at most once.
The panel's tab shows the plugin's name, "Notes", which the package lists.
The panel's frame, tab and close button are the dock's, and what is inside the frame is the plugin's.

A view's grid names the panel by the id of the plugin's class, as `{ "plugin": "blockr.notes-notes_plugin" }`.
An app script places the panel in a grid with `plg()`, as the vignette [Views and grids](layouts.html) shows.
The panel picker, which the "+" in the header of each tab group opens, lists after the blocks, under "Plugins", each plugin with a `ui` that the active view does not show.
A board that holds no view opens on the view "Page", whose left rail holds the panel of each of the app's plugins with a `ui`.
A plugin that no view of a saved board holds, such as one that the app added since the board was saved, shows in no panel until the user picks it from the panel picker or a command shows it.

The dock mounts the plugin's UI when it draws the panel.
It runs the cleanup that `render()` returned once the panel goes: when the user closes the panel's tab, when the active view changes to one that does not show the panel, or when another board opens.
Core aborts the signal of `render()` then too.
A panel behind another tab or on a collapsed rail stays mounted.
So the UI keeps what it holds outside the plugin's state, such as a scroll position or a note that the user has not saved yet.
The dock may mount the UI again, as when the user switches back to a view that shows the panel.
So a plugin keeps in its state what others should see, and runs from its class's `start` what has to outlive its panel.

## Sizing from its own element

The element in which the dock mounts the UI fills the panel's body, at the panel's width and height.
It scrolls where what the plugin draws is taller than the panel.
So a plugin sizes itself from its own element, with `height: 100%`, a container query or a `ResizeObserver`, as the Notes plugin shows the block of each note only where its panel is wide enough:

```css
.notes {
  container-type: inline-size;
}

.notes .note-block {
  display: none;
}

@container (min-width: 30rem) {
  .notes .note-block {
    display: inline;
  }
}
```

A collapsed rail shows its tabs alone, and the dock hides the panels on it rather than squeeze them.
So a plugin need not tell a collapsed rail from a narrow panel by its width.

A plugin draws only inside its element and in the browser's top layer.
Nothing that it draws depends on the dock's markup, such as the classes of the dock's frame or of dockview, which draws the dock's layout.
It gives no element an ID, since the whole page shares the IDs of its elements, as the UI of a block gives none either.
So it draws the same under every frontend.

## Room beyond the panel

A plugin that needs more room than its panel, as for a form or a menu, opens it in the browser's top layer.
A `<dialog>` that `showModal()` opens is in the top layer, and so is a popover.
Nothing on the page clips an element there, so the panel's edges do not cut it off.
The element still sits inside the plugin's element, so the cleanup removes it with the rest of the UI.
In the Notes plugin, the button `edit` opens a form in a dialog, and the button `more` opens a menu:

```ts
const dialog = document.createElement("dialog");
dialog.setAttribute("aria-label", "Edit note");
dialog.append(form);
el.append(dialog);
edit.addEventListener("click", () => dialog.showModal(), { signal });

const menu = document.createElement("div");
menu.popover = "auto";
el.append(menu);
more.popoverTargetElement = menu;
```

The button `more` opens and closes the menu through its `popoverTargetElement`, which needs no element ID.
The dock offers no place for dialogs or menus, and its own menus, such as the panel picker, are popovers too.

## Showing a block or a plugin

A plugin shows a block or a plugin through core's `show()`, as under every frontend:

```ts
await core.show({ block: note.block });
await core.show({ plugin: "blockr.dag-dag_plugin" });
```

Under the dock, `show()` takes these steps:

1. Core throws for a block that the board does not hold, and for a plugin that the app does not run or whose class has no `ui`.
2. Core gives a block focus, in `core.focus`.
3. Core calls the `show()` of the dock's frontend, which runs the dock's command `blockr.dock-show_panel` with the object, which names the panel as a grid names it.
4. Where the active view shows the panel, the tab group or rail that holds it brings its tab to the front, and a collapsed rail opens.
   While the board option `sync_rails` is on, the rail opens on every view that has a rail on that edge.
5. Where the active view does not show the panel, the command places it at the default place: a new tab in the last tab group that holds only blocks' panels.
   Where no tab group holds only blocks' panels, as in a view that shows nothing, the panel gets a new tab group at the end of the view's top split.
6. The promise resolves once the dock has shown the panel.

Showing takes no undo step, placing included, so the user's Undo passes over it.
It never switches views, and it leaves the keyboard's focus where it is.
On a locked board, the dock places no panel.
There `show()` brings forward only a panel that the active view shows, and otherwise resolves without showing anything, while core has given a block focus all the same.

## Reading the dock's state

The dock keeps its views, the folders that group them, the active view and the sections that each block's card shows in its plugin state.
The board holds that state under the id of the dock's class, `blockr.dock-dock_plugin`, open to every plugin, as the rest of the board is:

```ts
import type { Board } from "@blockr/core";

const DOCK = "blockr.dock-dock_plugin";

type View = {
  readonly name: string;
  readonly folder: string | null;
  readonly index: string;
  readonly grid: unknown;
};

type Folder = {
  readonly name: string;
  readonly folder: string | null;
  readonly index: string;
};

type DockState = {
  readonly views: Readonly<Record<string, View>>;
  readonly folders: Readonly<Record<string, Folder>>;
  readonly active: string | null;
  readonly visible: Readonly<Record<string, readonly ("inputs" | "outputs")[]>>;
};

function dockState(board: Board): DockState | undefined {
  return board.plugins[DOCK] as DockState | undefined;
}
```

The state has four parts:

- The part `views` holds each view by its id, with its `name`, the `folder` that it sits in, or `null` for the top of the views menu, its `index` and its `grid`.
- The part `folders` holds each folder by its id, with its `name`, its `folder` and its `index`.
- The part `active` holds the id of the active view.
- The part `visible` holds, by block id, the sections that a block's card shows, for each card that hides one.

The views menu orders the views and folders of each folder by their `index`, which it compares by code units.
A grid holds its top split, with its `orientation`, its `children` and their `sizes`, and its rails by edge in `rails`.
Each child is a split, with its own `children` and `sizes`, or a tab group, with its `panels` and the `active` one, which it shows.
A rail holds its `panels` and its `active` one too, whether it is `collapsed`, and its `size`, its width in pixels while it is open.
The schema of the state ships with the dock, as `js/dock.schema.json` in the installed package, and describes each field.

Under another frontend, the board holds no state for the dock, and `dockState()` above gives `undefined`.
A plugin follows the state as it changes through `core.store.subscribe()`, as it follows the rest of the board.
To tell which blocks and plugins the user sees, a plugin reads `core.onScreen` instead, and to tell which block the user works in, `core.focus`, since every frontend sets both.
Under the dock, `core.onScreen` holds the blocks and plugins whose panels the tab groups and the open rails of the active view show.

## Changing which views hold which panels

A plugin places a panel in a view, or takes one out of a view, with the dock's commands `blockr.dock-add_panel` and `blockr.dock-remove_panel`.
Any plugin runs them through `core.commands.run()`, as any package runs another's commands.

| Command | Args | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `blockr.dock-add_panel` | `view`, `panel`, and `near`, `side` or `rail` | Places a panel in a view that does not show it, as the tab that its tab group or rail shows |
| `blockr.dock-remove_panel` | `view`, `panel` | Takes a panel out of a view, as closing its tab does |

The arg `view` is the id of a view, and `panel` names the panel as a grid names it, as `{ "block": "a" }`.
Without `near`, `side` and `rail`, the panel goes to the default place, as for `show()`.
With `rail`, `"left"` or `"right"`, it goes on the rail at that edge of the view.
With `near`, a panel of the view, it goes in the tab group of that panel, or in a new tab group beside it, on the `side` given: `"left"`, `"right"`, `"above"` or `"below"`.
Each of the two commands is one undo step.
The command `blockr.dock-remove_panel` removes no block, and the other views that show the panel keep it.

A plugin draws a control for one of the dock's commands only where `core.commands.registered()` holds that command.
Another frontend registers none of the dock's commands, so there the plugin draws no such control and works on.
The plugin greys the control out where `core.commands.preflight()` fails, as for a view that shows the panel already, or on a locked board, where neither command runs.
As the Notes plugin draws the item of a note, it adds a button that puts the panel of the note's block on the right rail of the active view:

```ts
const ADD_PANEL = "blockr.dock-add_panel";

if (ADD_PANEL in core.commands.registered()) {
  const args = {
    view: dockState(core.store.board())?.active ?? null,
    panel: { block: note.block },
    rail: "right",
  };
  const pin = document.createElement("button");
  pin.textContent = "Pin to the right";
  pin.disabled = !core.commands.preflight(ADD_PANEL, args);
  pin.addEventListener("click", () => {
    core.commands.run(ADD_PANEL, args).catch(() => undefined);
  });
  item.append(pin);
}
```

The plugin draws its list again on every change of the board, a change of the active view included, so the button checks the preflight as it is drawn.

Where the command registry or the store refuses a command of the origin "user", core tells the user why, through a notification.
The call of `run()` still rejects, so the plugin catches the rejection and does nothing more.

The dock registers its other commands too, such as `blockr.dock-add_view` and `blockr.dock-move_panel`.
The command registry gives each with its label, a description of what it does and the schema of its args.
The guidance that the dock gives the assistant's model says how they fit together, in the file that `system.file("assistant", "skills", "layout", "SKILL.md", package = "blockr.dock")` gives.

## Settings

A plugin keeps a setting of its own in its state first, so that the setting saves and migrates with the plugin.
Its UI shows the setting and changes it through the plugin's commands, in its panel or in the top layer.
A board option is meant for how the board is shown, such as the dock's `view_tabs`, and is no substitute for that state.
A plugin's class names the board options of that kind that its plugin reads in R, through its method of `plugin_options()` (see `?blockr.core::plugin_options`).
Its package registers those that it ships (see `?blockr.core::new_board_option`).

The dock's options sidebar, which the options button in the navbar opens, shows each board option that the board holds, under its category.
It mounts the UI of each with `core.mountOption()`, a board option that a plugin requires among them.
It shows them on a locked board too, since the board lock leaves board options open.
So a plugin's board options need no place of their own, and they show under every frontend, as core's basic frontend shows them in its toolbar.

## No other place

Besides the panel, the dock draws what every frontend draws for plugins:

- The notifications of `CoreApi`, each by what it concerns.
  Those about a block show on the block's card, whoever raised them, a plugin included.
  A plugin shows those about itself in its panel, and while a warning or an error about the plugin holds, the dock draws a dot on the panel's tab, whose tooltip holds their messages.
  Where the active view holds no panel of the plugin, each notification about the plugin shows as a toast, with a link that shows the panel.
  Every other notification shows as a toast, such as one about the board or one about a plugin without a `ui`.
- The controls of the app's storage plugin, which its class's `storage` gives, show in the navbar, in the navbar's look.
  What the controls cannot hold, the storage plugin opens in a dialog of its own, in the top layer.

The navbar's other items are the app's.
An app script gives them to `serve()` in `navbar` (see `?default_navbar`), and no plugin adds to the navbar.

The dock offers plugins no other place.
Its block cards offer them no section, no button in a card's header and no item in a card's menu, and the dock gives them no panel for each block and no place for dialogs or menus.
So the dock declares no member of its own on core's `PluginClass`, and reads no member of a plugin's class beyond core's.
A plugin that draws in its panel and in the top layer, and works on the board through `CoreApi`, works the same under the dock as under core's basic frontend.
